Flooding along the banks of the Nullah Lai has been taking place for decades. If you visit the area today, you will notice that the people who live in its way have come up with ways to manage. House entrances are built two to three feet above ground in places such as Arya Mohalla and Muslim Colony and retaining walls have come up in places.

Nullah Lai flooded again this September, after over 200mm of rain in a single day. A week later its waters had receded from the low-lying neighbourhoods of Rawalpindi, but people were still struggling to cope. In Muslim Colony, Arya Muhalla and Dhoke Elahi Bakhsh water rose several feet, as evidenced by the level of damp that crawled up and stayed in the walls.

Shopkeepers in several areas were still trying to sort through their goods to see what could be salvaged. Outside one home, someone had placed their children’s toys out in the sun to dry.

Since the 1980s the authorities have been trying to find ways to cope. But it was only after the events of July 23, 2001 that efforts began in earnest. Rawalpindi usually receives 1,200-1,300 mm of rain a year. On that day, however, 620mm, half of the city’s annual rainfall, fell in 10 hours. Seventy-four people were killed, hundreds of houses and shops were inundated, and billions of rupees worth of property was ruined.

The government turned to the Japan International Cooperation Agency or JICA to make it a plan to deal with the nullah’s flooding (JICA had published one in 1987). It took roughly two years. In 2003, ‘The Study on Comprehensive Flood Mitigation and Environmental Improvement Plan of Lai Nullah Basin’ recommended short- to long-term solutions. Only the short-term option—the installation of an early warning system—was actually implemented. The rest was deemed impractical or not feasible enough.

A specialized unit to monitor the Nullah Lai was set up at the Pakistan Meteorological Department in 2006. The system was upgraded to an indigenous one in 2018, and upgraded again in 2025 with the help of Islamic Relief.

The Unit has advised evacuations 15 times since 2007. Alerts are sent out to Rescue 1122, whose members then make announcements for evacuations in local mosques.

The unit monitors data from seven rain gauges and two water level gauges installed along the Lai. Predictions are made using a formula in which upstream gauges such as those at Golra and Saidpur carry higher weightage, because that water will inevitably end downstream. The two water level gauges have cameras so the water is continuously monitored.

The management of the 234.8 square kilometer catchment area of Nullah Lai poses a more elementary governance problem. Over 144 sq km (61%) of the basin lies in Islamabad, which is upstream and faces less of a threat of urban flooding. On the other hand, Rawalpindi, a city older and more built up than Islamabad, has to contend with the water while located lower down.

When it rains, Rawalpindi’s residents don’t just need to look at the sky, they also need to look towards Islamabad. JICA highlighted this problem.

“The principal beneficiary of the proposed flood mitigation plan is biased to the lower reaches of Lai Nullah in Rawalpindi City, while the major flood mitigation structures such as the community pond and the diversion structure are placed in the upper reaches in Islamabad City,” the report said. “This contradiction may lead to conflicts between the regional administrators for the two cities in implementation and management of the proposed flood mitigation.”

Still JICA came up with a plan in 2003 that proposed canals to divert the water, dams to store it and a community pond. The Capital Development Authority came up with its own plan instead. Here’s how the two plans will work.

The dam in E-11 could not be built because five housing societies have since sprung up there. Then the CDA believes that the community pond risked raising the water table to a dangerously high level, which could flood F-8. Additionally, the diversion channels also risked raising water levels in the Korang River which could end up flooding the Islamabad Expressway, an important and busy road. In recent years, the Expressway has seen flooding, indicating the CDA might have been right.

So the CDA developed groundwater recharge wells in Sectors H and I. Initially one hundred wells were set up in 2022 after a pilot project with the Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources and more are in the works. The CDA has planned five water storage tanks at the base of the Margallah Hills. As for rainwater harvesting, it has been written into the city’s building codes but results will take time to show.

The CDA says Rawalpindi can do more to widen its channels and clean them. The Water and Sanitation Agency spent Rs60 million cleaning the nullah’s waterways ahead of the 2026 monsoon, but more funds are needed to do the task fully.

Rawalpindi’s main option is the Lai Expressway. The project was conceived in 2006 but despite early momentum, work was halted in 2008. Plans are once again underway to revive the project.

Apart from building a dual-lane expressway to ease traffic flows, the project aims to define the banks of the nullah and prevent encroachment. With retaining walls on each side, the expressway hopes to mitigate the effects of overflows in the stream.

In Rawalpindi, the NGO Shehersaz is already undertaking a rainwater harvesting project called PUCCAR in collaboration with the UN Habitat and the Adaptation Fund. They installed 2,276 units in seven union councils in Rawalpindi, primarily in places near streams. The water can be used for domestic purposes in areas which get supply once a day for a few minutes.

Meanwhile, JICA has signed another MoU with CDA. The 36-month project is aimed at developing an ‘integrated water supply, sewerage and drainage master plan’. CDA officials say that meetings with JICA representatives have stressed that the plans developed this time around must have better feasibility studies conducted so they can actually be put in place.
